column4: God creates the pairs and appoints ships and cattle as mounts, placing the section's worn mount inside a divinely furnished journey.
The rider settles on the mount's back and remembers the One who subjected it, correcting the possessive attachment that the section says trial wears away.
The mount prayer ends, “to our Lord we shall return,” joining vehicle, journey, and final return in one scene.
Every soul tastes death, is tested through evil and good, and is returned to God; this states the section's whole sequence of wearing trial and return.
A person at the edge is reassured by good but turns away under trial; this reverses the tranquil soul by exposing a calm dependent on fortune.
People are told to walk through the earth, eat God's provision, and know that resurrection is to Him; travel, provision, and destination form one itinerary.
“My servants” are told that God's earth is spacious and to worship Him, making movement through the earth the prelude to the section's final summons among the servants.
After the servants are told to move through God's broad earth in 29:56, every soul tastes death and is returned to Him.
The believers who travel, die, and return in 29:56-57 are lodged permanently in lofty Garden chambers, completing the journey with settlement.
God promises testing through fear, hunger, and loss of wealth and lives; trial literally diminishes what the traveler thought was his.
The tested people of 2:155 answer loss by saying they belong to God and are returning to Him, exactly joining attrition to return.
God tests a dispersed people with good and bad “so that they might return,” uniting both kinds of trial with return.
The call to set out asks why believers grow heavy toward the earth and prefer the nearer life; it names the section's grounded refusal of the journey.
The bearer of signs clings to the earth and follows desire, a direct Qur'anic realization of the section's earthbound animal and person.
Those fixed in their places can neither go forward nor return, directly staging the motionless mount and the blocked return together.
Human life is strenuous movement toward the Lord and ends in meeting Him, making the section's journey an account of all human effort.
Livestock carry burdens to a بلد reachable only with severe hardship, directly joining the section's land-word to a journey-worn carrier.
Pilgrims arrive on every lean camel from every distant pass; the lean body makes travel's wearing of the mount visible.
God places visible settlements along a measured route and commands safe travel through them by nights and days, a direct map of journey stages through lands.
The travelers ask that their journeys be lengthened and are scattered into tales, turning the measured road of 34:18 into loss and dispersal.
Moses refuses to stop until he reaches the meeting of the seas even if he travels for ages, opposing the section's creature that settles and will not rise.
After passing the appointed place, Moses explicitly says that the journey has caused weariness, the human counterpart to the worn mount.
Moses and his servant return along their own tracks, staging return as literal travel back toward a missed starting point.
God creates humans from earth, returns them into it, and brings them out again; return here is literally to the material point of beginning.
“As He began you, you will return” precisely matches the section's dictionary definition of return as going back to one's beginning.
Universal return to God is grounded in His beginning creation and repeating it, so destination and re-creation explain one another.
The challenge asks who begins creation and repeats it, then answers that God does; the root ع و د supplies return as renewed origin rather than mere reversal of direction.
God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, giving the journey's return a cosmic scale.
People are asked to see how God begins creation and repeats it; 29:20 then turns that insight into a journey through the earth.
The command to travel through the earth and observe how creation began links traversing lands to the final, next creation.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, an exact sequence from origin through return to destination.
God takes His servant by night from one sanctuary to another, the explicit Qur'anic night journey evoked by يَسْرِ.
Moses is commanded to take God's servants by night and strike a dry road through the sea, joining night departure, travelers, and an opened path.
Lot is told to take his family through part of the night without anyone turning back, making direction and forbidden reversal part of the nocturnal journey.
Lot is told to set out by night, follow behind his family, forbid backward looking, and proceed where commanded.
God commands Moses to take His servants by night because they will be pursued, casting the night journey as a departure under pressure.
The command to take God's servants by night because they will be pursued repeats the section's opening movement as a communal exodus.
The One who imposed the Qur'an promises the Prophet that He will return him to a مَعَاد, explicitly naming return as an appointed destination.
On that day the settled destination, ٱلْمُسْتَقَرّ, is to the Lord, so the journey ends in abiding before Him.
The warning “to your Lord is the return” addresses the self-sufficient transgressor, matching the section's return-address to the soul after worldly attachment.
The humble are certain both that they will meet their Lord and that they are returning to Him, combining the two ends named in 84:6 and the section.
Hearts find اطمئنان through God's remembrance, explicitly giving the source of the section's post-disturbance tranquility.
A heart remains مطمئن in faith even under coercion, showing tranquility that survives external disturbance rather than depending on ease.
Abraham asks to see how the dead are revived so that his heart may become tranquil, joining settled heart, death, and return to life.
Divine aid is made good news so that hearts may become tranquil through it, presenting calm as what follows fear and uncertainty.
The promise of angelic aid is given so hearts may become tranquil, again locating stillness after alarm in reliance on God.
The disciples seek the table so their hearts may become tranquil and certainty may follow their unsettled question.
Solomon names extraordinary provision as his Lord's test of gratitude or ingratitude, correcting the claim that bestowed abundance simply proves honor.
Believers are told that they will certainly be tested in their wealth and selves, the exact possessions and person that the section says trial abrades.
Wealth and children are identified as a trial, turning what people cling to into the very instrument of testing.
Wealth and children are only a trial, while the great reward is with God; possession becomes a stage rather than the destination.
Death and life are created to test which person acts best, placing the whole mortal journey inside a trial.
The owners of the garden are tested as earlier people were tested, and the owned garden becomes the means by which their claim to possession is worn down.
The earth's adornment is made a test of deeds, so attractive earthly possession is explicitly temporary testing material.
The bloom of worldly life given to groups is itself a test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Love of desires, including accumulated wealth and livestock, is worldly enjoyment, whereas the beautiful destination is with God.
Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes can be dearer than God and striving in His path; attachment directly prevents setting out.
Those who prefer the nearer life over the Hereafter also obstruct God's way, joining worldly preference to blockage of the road.
Choosing the nearer life over the Hereafter explains rejection, making misplaced love a decision about destination.
The rebuke says that people love the immediate life; 75:21 completes the motion by saying they leave the Hereafter behind.
Leaving the Hereafter accompanies love of the immediate in 75:20, showing how attachment determines which end of the journey is abandoned.
People love the immediate life and leave behind them a heavy day, combining attachment, neglect of the destination, and the section's imagery of weight.
The transgressor prefers the nearer life, the same choice named in the section's earthbound call.
Hell becomes the transgressor's shelter after his preference in 79:38, showing attachment ending in a contrary abode.
People prefer the nearer life, directly naming the choice that makes the traveler cling to the present ground.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting than what is preferred in 87:16, defining the true destination by permanence.
Worldly life is vegetation that flourishes after rain and then becomes wind-scattered debris, a visible account of what use and time wear away.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing what the traveler carries from what remains at arrival.
Worldly rivalry in wealth and children is compared to vegetation that delights, withers, yellows, and becomes debris; possession visibly ages like the section's garment and mount.
The human being's intense love of wealth directly repeats the attachment named in 89:20 before the surah turns to the graves.
Competitive accumulation distracts travelers from their end until the grave-visit of 102:2.
The distracted accumulators finally visit the graves, making death the unavoidable stop that wealth-love had hidden.
The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, enacting the clinging possessiveness of the section.
He imagines that wealth has made him permanent, a direct false reversal of the journey toward death and return.
Righteousness is not reached until people spend from what they love, turning release of attachment into forward movement.
True righteousness includes giving wealth despite love of it to kin, orphans, and the needy, reversing the section's conjunction of money-love and neglected dependents.
The righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite love of the food, showing love loosened rather than used as an anchor.
Thamud are made successors after Aad and settled in the earth, building palaces and carving mountain homes; the section's named nations, lands, and grounded settlement meet in one verse.
Salih tells Thamud that God produced them from earth and settled them in it, then calls them to seek forgiveness and turn to Him.
The dwellings of Aad and Thamud remain visible, yet Satan blocked them from the way despite their discernment; fixed habit becomes obstruction of the road.
Aad construct great works as though they might remain forever, giving monumental form to the desire to settle permanently in the passing world.
God destroyed towns around the hearers and varied the signs “so that they might return,” joining ruined lands like those in surah 89 to the call back.
Travelers are told to inspect the fate of stronger predecessors who cultivated and built the earth; settled power did not prevent the journey's end.
The God-fearing are conducted in companies to the Garden and told at its opened gates to enter forever, the section's final entry as a completed caravan.
After entering in 39:73, the travelers praise God and take their place wherever they wish in the Garden's land, explicitly turning arrival into settlement.
“My servants” are addressed with freedom from fear and grief, the communal welcome corresponding to the tranquil soul's address.
The servants addressed in 43:68 are identified as those who believed and submitted, specifying who receives the welcome.
The welcomed servants are commanded to enter the Garden rejoicing, closely matching “enter among My servants” and “enter My Garden.”
The promised traveler comes with a heart that repeatedly turns back, preparing the inner posture for the entry commanded in 50:34.
“Enter it in peace” names entry, safety, and the day of permanent abiding as the end of the returning heart's road.
Angels take the good in death, greet them with peace, and command them to enter the Garden, staging the section's final address at death.
The righteous are told to enter gardens in peace and security, a direct parallel to tranquil entry after the journey.
People once despised are commanded to enter the Garden without fear or grief, giving the lowly traveler the opposite of worldly humiliation.
Eternal gardens culminate in God being pleased with the faithful and their being pleased with Him, directly expanding رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً.
On the truthful's Day, eternal gardens accompany God's pleasure with them and their pleasure with Him, linking mutual satisfaction to final abode.
God's pleasure with the first believers and their pleasure with Him are joined to gardens beneath which rivers flow and permanent residence.
At the lasting abode the travelers say that no fatigue or weariness touches them, so the worn journey ends rather than beginning another.
The final limit is to the Lord, an exceptionally concise statement of where the section's road ends.
The believer contrasts the world's brief enjoyment with the Hereafter as the home of settled residence, distinguishing the roadside from the abode.
The Garden's people have the better settled place and the finer resting place, giving the journey a true rest rather than earthbound stagnation.
The return of all people is to God, followed by their reckoning, stating the compulsory homeward direction of the journey.
God gives life and death and to Him is the destination, linking the whole mortal interval to its terminus.
The question denies that humans were created pointlessly or would fail to be returned, making return the purpose-bearing completion of creation.
The believer asks why he should not worship his Creator when everyone will be returned to Him, relating origin, allegiance, and end.
God gives life and death and to Him people are returned, defining return across the full span of the journey.
The joyful worldling thought that he would never return, directly opposing the strenuous meeting with the Lord announced in 84:6.
At death the unbeliever asks his Lord to send him back, seeking another journey only when the allotted one has ended.
The answer is كَلَّا: the request of 23:99 is only a spoken word, and a barrier prevents return until resurrection.
When stationed before the Fire, the deniers wish to be sent back so they could respond differently, a failed request to reverse the finished route.
God says that if they were sent back they would return to what was forbidden, exposing moral repetition inside the desired physical return.
At judgment the guilty ask to be returned so they can act rightly, another final-arrival scene in which a new outward journey is too late.
Heaven's gates do not open and entry to the Garden is impossible until a camel enters a needle's eye; mount, gate, and denied entry meet in one reversal.
Disbelievers too are driven in groups and told to enter, but their caravan reaches Hell; its mirrored staging sharpens the destination in 39:73.
At the final upheaval prized pregnant camels are abandoned, showing that even the most valued mount and possession cannot be carried beyond the journey.
Pharaoh is again called “owner of the stakes,” confirming the stake as the emblem attached to the tyrant named in the section.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, extending the burden-bearing journey of 16:7 into its family of mounts.
Livestock give drink and many benefits, so the mount is also provision rather than merely property that belongs to its rider.
People are carried on livestock and ships, making the mortal traveler a passenger on means supplied to him.
God appoints livestock so that people ride some and eat from others, locating the mount among gifts rather than possessions secured by the self.
Needs are attained through livestock, and people are carried on them and on ships, broadening the section's one exhausted mount into all human transport.
The Qur'an directs attention to how the camel was created; the section's lexicographic camel-image thus points back to a creature made for contemplation.
The winter and summer journeys make repeated seasonal travel the condition of Quraysh's settled security and provision.
One who leaves home migrating to God and His messenger, then dies on the road, has already secured the reward; bodily travel can end before arrival while its direction remains decisive.
A near gain and moderate journey would have drawn the reluctant, but distance burdens them, revealing how worldly calculation arrests setting out.
Had the reluctant truly intended to set out, they would have prepared equipment; instead they are told to remain with those who sit.
Those left behind rejoice in sitting after the Messenger and dislike striving with wealth and selves, a social scene of attachment to place.
They are content to remain with those left behind, so consent itself becomes the fastening that keeps them from the road.
Those able to go nevertheless ask exemption and accept being among those left behind, repeating the grounded refusal knowingly.
The desert Arabs claim that wealth and families kept them occupied, giving possessions as the stated reason for remaining behind a commanded journey.
People are commanded to travel through the earth and see the end of deniers, reading ruined predecessors as stations of warning.
The command to journey through the earth and inspect the deniers' end makes travel itself a lesson in destination.
Travel through the earth is urged so that the end of earlier peoples can be seen, while the Hereafter is named as better for the God-fearing.
After recalling messengers sent to every community, the hearers are told to travel through the earth and see the deniers' end.
Journeying through the earth is meant to produce understanding hearts and hearing ears amid the remains of destroyed settlements.
Travel through the earth and observation of criminals' end turn the country-crossing traveler into a witness of where rebellion leads.
The command to travel and view earlier peoples' end connects traversal of countries with the repeated consequences of shirk.
Travel is commanded so people can see how stronger predecessors ended, denying that established power can halt the route to judgment.
Those who journey through the earth can see the end of predecessors stronger in power and traces, a parallel to surah 89's powerful ruined peoples.
Travelers are again told to inspect the fate of the more numerous and stronger predecessors whose acquisitions did not benefit them.
Travel through the earth reveals the destroyed end of earlier deniers and warns that present disbelief has the same destination.
God begins and repeats creation; the ع و د wording keeps the section's final return tied to renewal even without a travel scene.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting, distinguishing supplies from destination.
Whatever people receive is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
Those content with the nearer life become tranquil in it and neglect the signs; اطمئنان here is an earthbound settling opposite the Godward tranquil soul.
The one brought near receives rest and fragrant provision, preparing the Garden welcome stated in 56:89.
At death the near one is received with rest, fragrance, and a Garden of bliss, a compact arrival after mortal exertion.
Joseph tells his traveling family to enter Egypt safely, a worldly reunion and secure entry that can illuminate the form, though not the final object, of the section's welcome.
On the final day criminals are seen bound together in fetters, giving the binding side of the section's journey-image its punitive destination.
The condemned is seized and shackled at arrival, the immobilized opposite of the tranquil soul freely commanded to enter.
He is inserted into a long chain, completing the binding sequence begun in 69:30.
Chains, shackles, and a blaze await rejecters, turning the section's brief binding image into a final state of enforced immobility.
The earth casts out its burdens at the last convulsion, reversing the person who tried to grow heavy and remain attached to it.
The people of the lasting Garden are clothed in silk after arrival; this may faintly reverse the source section's dictionary image of a garment worn out by use.

A secure, tranquil town receives ample provision from every direction, then ingratitude makes it taste the “garment” of hunger and fear; tranquility, provision, trial, settlement, and worn clothing converge.
Abraham asks for a secure بلد and provision, while God says the unbeliever receives brief enjoyment before being driven to the Fire, joining settlement and supplies to divergent destinations.
The command to set out light or heavy directly answers the earthward heaviness of 9:38 and makes weight no excuse for remaining fixed.
God guides to Himself whoever turns back to Him; this Godward turning immediately precedes the heart's tranquility in 13:28.
Those whose hearts become tranquil in 13:28 receive blessedness and a beautiful homecoming, so inner rest points toward final settlement.
The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing rather than remaining distant, beginning the arrival scene completed by entry in 50:34.
The promised Garden belongs to every repeatedly returning, watchful person, identifying return as the disposition of the traveler welcomed in 50:33-34.
Believing servants are told to fear their Lord and reminded that God's earth is spacious, making migration through the earth part of faithful perseverance.
When hardship touches a person he calls on God, but after a favor he claims it came through his own knowledge; God calls the favor itself a test.
The question challenges the belief that continued wealth and sons necessarily signify favor, directly exposing the error dramatized in 89:15.
What people mistake for hastened good in 23:55 is explicitly denied, separating bestowed abundance from divine approval.
The affluent claim that superior wealth and children mean they will not be punished, the same false inference from provision to honor.
The Prophet is told to answer that God expands and restricts provision as He wills, directly matching the two conditions misread in 89:15-16.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and action, rather than possessions, determine nearness and reward.
A person tirelessly asks for good but becomes despairing when adversity touches him, exposing a soul whose state is governed by provision.
After mercy follows adversity, the person calls it his own, doubts the Hour, and assumes a fine return, combining possession, denial of the journey's end, and false confidence.
The human being is created anxiously unstable, introducing the opposed reactions to adversity and good in 70:20-21.
When harm touches him he panics, paralleling the mistaken humiliation inferred from restricted provision.
When good touches him he withholds it, joining favorable provision to the clinging refusal to release possessions.
The recipient of wealth is told to seek the Hereafter through what God gave while using his worldly share well, turning possession into provisions for the destination.
Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, making worldly attachment culminate in literal earthward engulfment.
After Qarun's fall, his former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that abundance did not prove favor.
The garden owner enters his possession and asserts that it will never perish, treating a temporary station as permanent settlement.
He doubts the Hour yet assumes that, if returned to his Lord, he will find an even better destination, corrupting return into entitlement.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, visibly wearing away what he thought securely his.
The tested owners' garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, making the attrition announced in 68:17 visible.
The owners finally confess that they have been deprived, discovering through loss that possession and provision were never guaranteed.

Abraham settles descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks that hearts incline toward them, and asks for provision, joining settlement, attachment, and sustenance without confusing any with the final home.
Those who denied meeting God arrive suddenly at the Hour carrying their burdens on their backs, turning the journey's figurative load into a final visible weight.
No burdened soul bears another's load, even a heavily laden person cannot transfer it, and the verse ends by naming God as the destination.
No burden-bearer carries another's burden, establishing the personal load whose corresponding effort is named in 53:39.
A human being has only what he strives for, closely paralleling the strenuous movement toward the Lord in 84:6.
Each person's striving will be seen, so no stage of the journey's labor disappears at arrival.
The seen striving is fully repaid before 53:42 names the Lord as the final limit.
Those who strive toward God are promised guidance along His ways, joining exertion, direction, and divine accompaniment.
“Flee to God” turns return into urgent directed motion and identifies God Himself as refuge and destination.
Believers are commanded to race toward forgiveness and a Garden, giving the final abode the force of a destination actively approached.
The command to race toward forgiveness and the Garden casts faithful life as a contest whose finish is divine pardon and abode.
Every soul is told to inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, making deeds advance provisions to the destination before the traveler arrives.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and then reaches Hell, showing worldly preference determining a ruinous endpoint.
Whoever wants the Hereafter, strives toward it properly, and believes has that striving accepted, supplying the positive route opposite 17:18.
The person who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire, reversing the worldly preference described in 79:38.
The Garden becomes the shelter of the desire-restraining traveler, completing the alternative destination to 79:39.
Angels descend upon the steadfast, remove fear and grief, and announce the promised Garden, a close communal parallel to the tranquil soul's final welcome.
The greatest terror does not grieve the faithful; angels receive them with the announcement that this is their promised day.
The God-fearing are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, a dignified caravan that sharpens the companies driven to the Garden.
Criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, providing the opposed caravan and destination to the delegation in 19:85.
The God-fearing are promised a beautiful homecoming, naming the quality of the destination before its doors appear in 38:50.
Everlasting gardens stand with their gates opened to the arriving God-fearing, paralleling the opened-gate entry in 39:73.
The Garden's people suffer no fatigue and are never expelled, so arrival ends both weariness and further forced travel.
Those abiding in Paradise desire no transfer from it, explicitly marking the destination as the end of relocation.
The slain believer is directly told to enter the Garden, a singular death-side welcome closely parallel to the soul's command in surah 89.
The recipient of the right-hand record enters a “pleasing life,” echoing the root of the pleased soul at arrival.
That pleasing life is located in a lofty Garden, supplying the abode for the satisfaction named in 69:21.
The arrivals eat and drink because of what they sent ahead in past days, presenting final provision as the fruit of advance preparation.
Radiant faces are pleased with their striving, joining arduous effort to satisfaction at its result.
Those pleased with their striving in 88:9 are in a lofty Garden, locating that satisfaction at the journey's end.
God addresses prodigal people as “My servants” and forbids despair, opening a return while the journey can still change.
The servants are commanded to turn back to their Lord and submit before punishment arrives, the timely counterpart to the denied request in 23:99.
When judgment's interpretation arrives, deniers ask either for intercessors or to be returned so they can act differently, another too-late attempt to reverse the route.
The inhabitants of the Fire cry to be taken out so they can act rightly, but their completed lifespan and warning make the requested new journey unavailable.
After confessing two deaths and two lives, the condemned ask whether there is any path out, explicitly seeking a road away from the final destination.
When wrongdoers see punishment they ask whether there is any way of return, a final search for a road back after arrival.
At the coming of death, a person asks for a short delay in order to give and become righteous, seeking extra travel-time only at the endpoint.
God never delays a soul when its appointed time arrives, closing the extension requested in 63:10.
The condemned wish for one more return so they could become believers, stating the impossible repeated journey in a single request.
God sends the she-camel itself as a test, unexpectedly joining the section's camel image to its explicit theme of trial.
Shackles reaching to the chins hold rejecters with heads forced up, giving the section's binding image a scene of bodily immobilization.
God could efface their eyes so they race blindly for the path and cannot see it; 36:67 then removes even their power to advance or return.
Believers who sit without disability are not equal to those who strive with wealth and lives, making grounded nonmovement morally legible without condemning the unable.
Believers are explicitly told not all to set out; some remain to learn and warn their people, setting a boundary between necessary staying and earthbound refusal.
When God returns the Prophet to some who stayed behind, they are barred from future departure because they chose sitting the first time.
When commanded to believe and strive, the affluent ask permission to remain with those who sit, specifying privilege as a source of grounded refusal.
When mercy is withdrawn after being tasted, the human being becomes despairing and ungrateful, one half of the unstable reading of trial.
When favor follows adversity, the person exults that troubles have left and becomes boastful, completing the fortune-governed response begun in 11:9.
When warning is forgotten, every door of abundance is opened until people rejoice, then they are seized suddenly; provision functions as concealed testing.
God afflicts towns that rejected prophets with hardship so they might humble themselves, making constriction an invitation rather than proof of humiliation.
God replaces adversity with prosperity before seizing the heedless, so both conditions reveal rather than certify divine approval.
Those who desire worldly life and adornment may receive the full return of their deeds within it, but that payment does not make it the final abode.
The world-seekers of 11:15 have only Fire in the Hereafter, exposing the destination hidden by complete worldly payment.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who wants only the nearer life, identifying exclusive worldly desire as a refusal of further direction.
Seeking the Hereafter's harvest increases it, while seeking the world's harvest yields a portion with no share in the Hereafter; desire selects what the journey produces.
God carries Adam's children on land and sea and provides good things, framing human mobility and supplies as conferred honor rather than ownership.
Travelers in a ship call sincerely on God in danger, then associate partners after He delivers them to land, so safe ground becomes the place of renewed forgetfulness.
Some people travel through the earth seeking God's bounty, a direct Qur'anic instance of the country-crossing traveler whose road is tied to provision.
After creation and death, some people are returned to decrepit age, making bodily life itself a wearing process rather than a secure possession.
God creates from weakness, grants strength, then returns strength to weakness and gray age, describing the traveler's embodied arc as renewed attrition.
Whoever is granted long life is reversed in creation, a bodily counterpart to the mount and garment worn through continued use.
Humanity is created in toil, supporting the section's presentation of mortal life as an arduous passage rather than settled ease.
When one task is finished, the addressee is told to continue laboring, keeping exertion continuous until its orientation is named in 94:8.
Desire is directed toward the Lord after renewed labor in 94:7, assigning the traveler's effort its proper end.
The patient are rewarded with a lofty chamber and received there with greeting and peace, another final welcome after endurance.
Their dwelling is permanent and praised as both settlement and residence, distinguishing arrival from a temporary stop.
Patience is rewarded with a Garden and silk, allowing the source section's worn mount and garment to end in enduring shelter and clothing.
God is pleased with the faithful and they are pleased with Him, and they are named God's party, extending mutual satisfaction beyond solitary feeling into belonging.
Pharaoh's wife asks her Lord to build her a house near Him in the Garden, defining final settlement by nearness to the Lord rather than earthly palace.
On the true Day, whoever wills is invited to take a homeward course toward the Lord, expressing destination as a route deliberately chosen.
God guides the human being to the way and leaves gratitude or ingratitude as the response, joining direction to the trial of received gifts.
On the great emergence a person remembers what he strove for, bringing the whole road's effort into awareness before the two destinations are disclosed.
The one whose destination is Fire is first identified by transgression, supplying the moral movement behind the worldly preference of 79:38.
The person with heavy scales enters a pleasing life, a further use of satisfaction for the state reached after judgment.
